gloss_terse: Aijalon — a Levitical city in the territory of Dan, in the valley where Joshua commanded the moon to stand still
gloss_readable: The place name אַיָּלוֹן (Aijalon), likely derived from אַיָּל (deer/stag), designates a city in the Shephelah foothills allotted to the tribe of Dan and later assigned as a Levitical city. Its fame rests on Joshua's dramatic command: 'Moon, stand still over the valley of Aijalon' (Josh 10:12). The Amorites retained control for some time, as the Danites struggled to dispossess them (Judg 1:35). It later served as a fortified city under Rehoboam (2 Chr 11:10) and was seized by the Philistines in Ahaz's day (2 Chr 28:18). Spanish 'Ajalón' and English 'Aijalon' both transliterate the Hebrew directly.

senses.1: A city in the Shephelah foothills within Dan's tribal allotment, identified with modern Yalo northwest of Jerusalem. Best known from Joshua's battlefield prayer for the moon to halt over its valley (Josh 10:12). Listed among Dan's cities (Josh 19:42), assigned to the Kohathite Levites (Josh 21:24; 1 Chr 6:69), and mentioned in the Amorite resistance narrative (Judg 1:35). Later fortified by Rehoboam (2 Chr 11:10) and lost to Philistine raids under Ahaz (2 Chr 28:18). Spanish 'Ajalón' and French 'Ayyalôn' preserve the Semitic form.

gloss_terse: Where? — interrogative adverb of place, demanding identification of a location or situation
gloss_readable: The interrogative adverb אֵיפֹה (eifoh) asks 'where?' with a directness that often carries emotional or theological weight beyond mere geography. When Joseph asks shepherds 'where are they pasturing?' (Gen 37:16), the question launches the pivotal narrative of his descent into Egypt. Ruth's mother-in-law Naomi asks 'where did you glean today?' (Ruth 2:19), probing for evidence of providential care. Most dramatically, God challenges Job: 'Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation?' (Job 38:4), using the spatial question to expose the gulf between divine and human knowledge. Spanish '¿dónde?' and French 'où?' capture the interrogative force.

senses.1: An interrogative adverb meaning 'where?' used to inquire about location, often with narrative or theological significance beyond the literal question. Joseph uses it to seek his brothers' whereabouts (Gen 37:16), Naomi uses it to discover Ruth's benefactor (Ruth 2:19), and God deploys it as a devastating rhetorical weapon against Job (Job 38:4). Also appears in Isaiah 49:21 and Judges 8:18. The compound form (אֵי + פֹּה, 'where here?') intensifies the immediacy. Spanish '¿dónde?' and German 'wo?' reflect the direct interrogative sense.

gloss_terse: Eliel — theophoric personal name meaning 'my God is God,' borne by at least nine men in Chronicles
gloss_readable: The name אֱלִיאֵל (Eliel) combines אֵל (God) twice in the construct 'my God is God,' a confession of exclusive devotion. It is borne by multiple individuals in the Chronicler's genealogies and military lists, making precise identification challenging. Notable bearers include a Manassite clan chief (1 Chr 5:24), two Benjaminites (1 Chr 8:20, 22), at least two of David's mighty warriors (1 Chr 11:46-47), a Gadite fighter (1 Chr 12:12), and Levites involved in the ark's transport (1 Chr 15:9, 11). Spanish 'Eliel' and English 'Eliel' both transliterate without alteration.

senses.1: A theophoric personal name meaning 'my God is God' or 'God is my God,' carried by multiple individuals concentrated in the books of Chronicles. These include a Manassite chief (1 Chr 5:24), Benjaminite heads of households (1 Chr 8:20, 22), warriors among David's elite (1 Chr 11:46-47; 12:12), and Levites who assisted in moving the ark (1 Chr 15:9, 11). The name's frequency in post-exilic genealogies reflects the Chronicler's concern for Israelite identity. Spanish and English both preserve the transliteration 'Eliel' unchanged.

gloss_terse: Immer — priestly family name; a priestly course and its descendants from the temple through the post-exilic period
gloss_readable: The name אִמֵּר (Immer) designates one of the twenty-four priestly courses organized under David (1 Chr 24:14) and the family descended from it. Members of the house of Immer appear throughout Israel's cultic history: serving in the pre-exilic temple (1 Chr 9:12; Jer 20:1, where Pashhur son of Immer is 'chief officer in the house of the LORD'), returning from Babylonian exile in significant numbers (Ezra 2:37; Neh 7:40 — over a thousand men), and dealing with the mixed-marriage crisis (Ezra 10:20). A locality called Immer is also mentioned among places from which returning exiles could not verify their Israelite ancestry (Ezra 2:59; Neh 7:61).

senses.1: A priestly family name tracing to the sixteenth of David's twenty-four priestly courses (1 Chr 24:14). Pashhur son of Immer served as chief temple officer and clashed with Jeremiah (Jer 20:1). The family returned from exile in large numbers — 1,052 men (Ezra 2:37; Neh 7:40) — and some were implicated in the foreign-wives controversy (Ezra 10:20). The name also appears as a place of uncertain location from which exiles returned without genealogical proof (Ezra 2:59; Neh 7:61). Spanish 'Imer' and English 'Immer' both transliterate the Hebrew.

gloss_terse: Ephrathah — region near Bethlehem; associated with Rachel's burial and the Messiah's birthplace (Mic 5:2)
gloss_readable: The name אֶפְרָתָה (Ephrathah) designates a district closely identified with Bethlehem in Judah, though the precise relationship — whether Ephrathah is an older name for Bethlehem itself or a surrounding region — remains debated. Rachel died and was buried on the road to Ephrath (Gen 35:16, 19; 48:7), establishing a link between this place and maternal grief. Ruth 4:11 pairs Ephrathah with Bethlehem in a blessing formula. Most significantly, Micah 5:2 prophesies that from 'Bethlehem Ephrathah' will come a ruler whose origins are from of old — a passage applied messianically in Matthew 2:6. The gentilic 'Ephrathite' (1 Sam 17:12) identifies David's family. Spanish 'Efrata' and French 'Éphrata' preserve the name across traditions.

senses.1: A place name closely associated with or identical to Bethlehem in Judah, carrying deep patriarchal and messianic significance. Rachel was buried on the road to Ephrath (Gen 35:16, 19; 48:7). Boaz's townsmen invoke it alongside Bethlehem in blessing Ruth's marriage (Ruth 4:11). Psalm 132:6 recalls finding the ark 'in the fields of Jaar' after hearing of it 'in Ephrathah.' Micah 5:2 names 'Bethlehem Ephrathah' as the birthplace of the future ruler, a prophecy central to Christian messianic expectation (Matt 2:6). Spanish 'Efrata' and German 'Ephrata' faithfully transmit the toponym.

gloss_terse: Lion (Aramaic) — the great predatory feline, appearing in Daniel's lion-den narrative and apocalyptic visions
gloss_readable: The Aramaic noun אַרְיֵה (aryeh) is the cognate of Hebrew אַרְיֵה and denotes the lion, the apex predator of the ancient Near East. All ten occurrences cluster in the book of Daniel. The lion-den narrative (Dan 6:7-24) uses the word repeatedly as Daniel is cast among lions whose mouths God shuts, then as those same lions devour his accusers — a vivid demonstration of divine sovereignty over nature's most fearsome beast. In Daniel 7:4, the first of four apocalyptic beasts rising from the sea is 'like a lion' with eagle's wings, symbolizing the Babylonian empire. Spanish 'león/leones' and French 'lion(s)' render the term directly.

senses.1: The lion as a literal animal in the Aramaic portions of Daniel, appearing exclusively in two contexts: the den of lions into which Daniel is thrown by royal decree and from which God delivers him by sending an angel to shut the lions' mouths (Dan 6:7, 12, 16-17, 19-20, 22, 24, 27), and the apocalyptic vision where the first beast resembles a lion with eagle's wings (Dan 7:4), widely understood as representing Babylon. Spanish 'león,' French 'lion,' and Arabic 'asad' all map to this apex predator of the ancient Levantine world.

gloss_terse: Artaxerxes — Persian royal name; the Achaemenid king(s) under whom Ezra and Nehemiah served
gloss_readable: The name אַרְתַּחְשַׁשְׂתְּא (Artachshasta), rendered 'Artaxerxes' following the Greek form, identifies one or possibly two Persian monarchs who authorized Jewish restoration projects. Artaxerxes I Longimanus (465-424 BCE) is most commonly identified: he commissioned Ezra's mission to restore Torah observance (Ezra 7:1, 7, 11-12) and granted Nehemiah leave to rebuild Jerusalem's walls (Neh 2:1; 5:14; 13:6). The name also appears in the correspondence of Ezra 4:7-23, where opponents appeal to the king to halt rebuilding. Spanish 'Artajerjes' and French 'Artaxerxès' both derive from the Greek intermediary rather than the Aramaic original.

senses.1: The Persian royal name Artaxerxes, referring primarily to Artaxerxes I Longimanus (465-424 BCE), the Achaemenid emperor who authorized both Ezra's priestly-scribal mission to Jerusalem (Ezra 7:1, 7, 11-12, 21) and Nehemiah's governorship and wall-building project (Neh 2:1; 5:14; 13:6). Also appears in the adversarial correspondence of Ezra 4:7-8, 11, 23, where provincial officials persuade the king to suspend Jewish construction. Spanish 'Artajerjes,' English 'Artaxerxes,' and German 'Artaxerxes' all derive from the Greek Ἀρταξέρξης rather than the Semitic form.

gloss_terse: Furnace (Aramaic) — the blazing kiln or smelting furnace, used of the fiery furnace in Daniel 3
gloss_readable: The Aramaic noun אַתּוּן (attun) designates a large furnace or kiln heated to extreme temperatures. All ten occurrences appear in Daniel 3, where Nebuchadnezzar orders Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego thrown into a furnace of blazing fire for refusing to worship his golden image. The furnace is heated 'seven times more than usual' (Dan 3:19), so hot it kills the soldiers who throw the three in (Dan 3:22). Yet Nebuchadnezzar sees four figures walking unharmed in the flames (Dan 3:25). The word cognates with Hebrew אָתוֹן (oven/furnace) and Akkadian utūnu. Spanish 'horno' and French 'fournaise' both capture the industrial-scale heat implied.

senses.1: A large furnace or kiln capable of producing intense heat, used exclusively in Daniel 3's narrative of the three Jewish exiles' ordeal. The furnace (אַתּוּן דִּי נוּרָא יָקִדְתָּא, 'furnace of blazing fire') functions as Nebuchadnezzar's instrument of execution for those who defy his idolatrous decree (Dan 3:6, 11, 15, 17, 20-21, 23, 26). The miraculous deliverance — four figures walking unscathed amid the flames — transforms the furnace from a symbol of tyrannical power to a witness of divine sovereignty. Spanish 'horno ardiente' and German 'Feuerofen' convey the terrifying scale.

gloss_terse: Alone, solitary, isolated — describing a state of separation, whether dignified independence or desolate loneliness
gloss_readable: The adjective/adverb בָּדָד (badad) describes the state of being alone, apart, or isolated. Its semantic range stretches from noble separateness to devastating loneliness. Balaam's oracle celebrates Israel as 'a people dwelling alone, not reckoning itself among the nations' (Num 23:9) — solitude as election. Moses' farewell blesses Israel: 'so Israel dwells in safety, alone' (Deut 33:28), and Deuteronomy 32:12 recalls that 'the LORD alone guided him.' Yet Lamentations opens with the agonized cry: 'How lonely sits the city that was full of people!' (Lam 1:1), where the same word expresses utter desolation. Spanish 'solo/solitario' and French 'seul/isolé' reflect this polarity.

senses.1: The state of being alone, solitary, or set apart, spanning a semantic range from honorable distinctness to grievous isolation. Positively: Israel dwells 'alone' as a people chosen and separated unto God (Num 23:9; Deut 33:28), and the LORD 'alone' led Israel through the wilderness (Deut 32:12). Negatively: Jerusalem sits 'alone' like a widow in her desolation (Lam 1:1), and Jeremiah sat 'alone' under the weight of prophetic burden (Jer 15:17). Leviticus 13:46 prescribes that the leper 'shall dwell alone.' Spanish 'solo/solitario' and English 'alone/solitary' capture both poles.

gloss_terse: Breach, gap, crack — structural damage in a wall or building requiring repair, especially in temple restoration
gloss_readable: The noun בֶּדֶק (bedeq) denotes a breach, crack, or gap in a structure — the kind of deterioration that demands masonry repair. Nearly all occurrences concentrate in 2 Kings 12, where young King Joash organizes the financing and execution of temple repairs after years of neglect under previous regimes. The repeated phrase בֶּדֶק הַבַּיִת ('breach of the house/temple') becomes almost a technical term for structural restoration work. Ezekiel 27:9 and 27:27 extend the image to ship-caulking, where Byblos's elders repair the 'breaches' of Tyre's merchant vessels. Spanish 'grieta/reparación' and English 'breach/repair' both oscillate between the damage and its remedy.

senses.1: A breach, crack, or structural gap in a building — especially the Jerusalem temple — requiring professional repair. Dominates 2 Kings 12:5-12 (paralleled in 2 Chr 24:4-12), where Joash directs priestly and artisan labor to mend the temple's deterioration (בֶּדֶק הַבַּיִת). Also used of ship-caulking in Ezekiel 27:9, 27, where the craftsmen of Gebal repair the 'seams' or 'leaks' of Tyre's trading fleet. The term thus spans architectural and nautical maintenance contexts. Spanish 'grietas del templo' and French 'brèches' convey the sense of structural damage awaiting restoration.
